title: The $151,000 Mortgage Shock Explained
hook_text: YOU PAY $151K BUT ONLY LOWER DEBT $25K

beats.say: You pay $151,000 on a $400,000 home loan, but your debt drops by just $25,500.
beats.visual: A cinematic overhead shot of a dark wooden desk with house keys sitting beside a calculator and a fountain pen, moody dramatic side lighting.

beats.say: Here's the exact math behind where your hard earned money actually goes in the first 5 years.
beats.visual: A silhouette of a person standing at a high-rise floor-to-ceiling glass window looking out at a dimly lit city skyline at dusk.

beats.say: Imagine buying a $400,000 house with a 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.5% interest.
beats.visual: A cinematic low-angle shot of a newly built modern residential suburban house exterior during golden hour, long shadows across the front yard.

beats.say: Your monthly payment for principal and interest comes out to exactly $2,528.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up of a hand stamping a dark blue ink stamp onto a thick blank beige paper document on a mahogany desk.

beats.say: You make every payment on time for 5 straight years, totaling $151,000 paid.
beats.visual: A macro shot of a sleek brass physical calendar flip-desk clock shifting through days, moody shadow cast across dark leather surface.

beats.say: You check your balance expecting a huge dent, but you still owe $374,500.
beats.visual: Close-up from behind of a person holding a plain off-white paper statement in hand, sitting in a dimly lit library chair.

beats.say: Out of that $151,000, roughly $25,500 went to principal, while over $126,000 went to interest.
beats.visual: A cinematic split-composition of two stacks of clean dark metal coins on a dark marble table, one tall stack and one very small stack.

beats.say: This isn't an artificial scheme—it's simple mathematics based on your outstanding loan balance.
beats.visual: An architect's desk with blueprint rolls, brass compasses, and a vintage magnifying glass under warm desk lamp illumination.

beats.say: Interest is charged on your remaining balance, which is naturally highest at the very start.
beats.visual: A moody close-up shot of a balance scale resting on a wooden tabletop, tilting heavily to one side in deep shadows.

beats.say: Because your balance is highest early on, over 83% of your early payments cover interest.
beats.visual: A dark glass hour-glass filled with metallic sand slowly trickling through the narrow middle section in slow motion.

beats.say: Adding small extra principal payments early reduces that base balance, saving tens of thousands later.
beats.visual: A person's hands writing with a gold pen on a clean, blank leather journal next to a cup of dark coffee.

beats.say: Knowing how debt works gives you total control over building real property equity.
beats.visual: A wide cinematic shot of a person standing atop a stone ridge overlooking a quiet foggy valley at sunrise, shot from behind.

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: A slow push-in shot of an elegant dark leather-bound book lying closed on a dark wooden table in a quiet study.

caption: Where does your mortgage money actually go? Here is the exact 5-year math breakdown.
description: Analyzing a $400,000 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.5% interest reveals that early payments primarily cover interest because the starting principal balance is at its highest. Understanding how interest calculations work allows homeowners to strategically pay down principal faster.
first_comment: Did you know how much of your early mortgage payment actually goes to interest?

facts.claim: On a $400,000 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.5%, monthly payment is $2,528 and total paid over 5 years is roughly $151,000.
facts.basis: Standard amortization math: 360 monthly payments of $2,528.27; 60 payments equal $151,696.

facts.claim: After 5 years, roughly $25,500 goes to principal and over $126,000 goes to interest.
facts.basis: Standard amortization breakdown: total principal paid in months 1-60 is $25,525; interest paid is $126,171.

facts.claim: Interest is charged on the remaining balance, which is naturally highest at the start of the loan.
facts.basis: Standard interest compounding math where monthly interest = (remaining principal * annual rate) / 12.
